blocks.p: Tanizaki's message came in the middle of the afternoon. It was four words long and it asked Rei to come now. Rei took the Keihin-Tōhoku line north from Ōji, the train with the sky-blue stripe. In Obon week it was full of people going home to their families. A man in a short-sleeved shirt slept against the window with a box of sweets on his knees, wrapped in shop paper for somebody's grandmother. Two schoolgirls shared one pair of earphones and laughed at the same moment. At Higashi-Jūjō the doors opened, and the heat came in with the noise of the cicadas in the trees beside the tracks.

He got off at Akabane. His Suica card beeped at the gate, and he walked out into the smell of hot concrete and frying oil from the station shops. The streets grew quieter as he went north. Some houses had white paper lanterns hanging by the door. A white lantern meant a family whose person had died in the past year, and who would come home this Obon for the first time. Near here the Sumida river splits away from the bigger Arakawa and begins its long run down through the city. Tanizaki's tea shop stood two streets from that water. Its shutter was down, with a handwritten card taped to it saying the shop was closed for the holiday. Rei went round to the side door and climbed the narrow stairs.

Tanizaki Seiichi was an old man of the Grid, the loose network of unregistered practitioners who worked outside the CVD. He had taught Gin most of what Gin knew about field work. He did not charge cash for anything. He charged in trust, and he spent it carefully.

blocks.cap: Tanizaki Seiichi, who pours before he speaks

blocks.p: Tanizaki poured before he spoke. That was how Rei knew the matter was serious. The old man had spent forty years in Kita, and he had learned that nothing true gets said over an empty cup. He never wasted the gesture on small business. The room above the shop smelled of roasted barley tea. It also smelled of the river two streets over, the brown smell of low tide and lantern wax that the whole district carried during Obon. Light came through the paper screens the colour of weak tea.
He set Rei's cup down with both hands and folded his own hands around his.
"A man went into the Sumida three nights ago," he said. "He has not come up."
Rei waited. Tanizaki did not like to be hurried, and he did not like to be helped.
"It is not a police matter. It will not become one." The old man looked at the steam, not at Rei. "I need him found before the river gives him up on its own terms."

The drowned man's name was Kase. He was a fixer on the Grid side. He was careful and unregistered, a go-between who arranged for a thing to change hands without either hand being seen. Tanizaki had used him for thirty years. He trusted him so much that he had stopped noticing him, the way a man stops noticing a good tool. Three nights ago Kase had sent word that he was holding something that frightened him. He wanted it out of his hands and into Tanizaki's before Obon reached its height. Then he sent nothing more. A Grid courier went to his flat and found it aired and empty. The kettle was still warm. His shoes stood paired by the door.

"A man does not walk to the river barefoot in this season by accident," Tanizaki said. He turned his cup a quarter-turn on the table and did not drink. "And the Sumida in Obon does not keep what it takes in the ordinary way. It launches the dead all week. I would rather find Kase before the river decides he is one of them."

Both of Rei's registers stirred at that. They always moved, low and slow, when something true was being made to sound smaller than it was. Tanizaki was not asking him to bring back a body. He was asking him to read one. He knew what reading a drowned man this week would pull through Rei, and he was asking anyway, and that told Rei how frightened he was. Tanizaki was the one person in Kita who never spent Rei carelessly. He had trained Gin with exactly this kind of restraint. Now he was pushing a cup across the table and asking for something he wanted kept off the official books. Whatever Kase had been carrying, it reached further than one fixer's bad night by the water.
The rain had not started. Down by the embankment, the first lantern sellers were setting out their paper boats.

Rei waited in the room until dark, because what he needed to see could only be seen at night. Then he walked the two streets to the river. Families were coming the same way, carrying lanterns and lighters and bottles of cold tea. A grandfather held a small boy on his shoulders, and the boy held the lantern. Somebody's radio was playing a sad old ballad. Moths circled the street lights, and the air was so wet that Rei's shirt stuck to his back after a hundred steps.

After dark the river was a black road carrying small fires. Tōrō nagashi had begun upstream. It is the Obon custom of floating lanterns on a river to guide the dead back to the other side. Each lantern was a paper box with a candle inside and a name brushed on the side. A family wrote the name, lit the candle and set the box on the water, and the current carried their dead away, gently, toward the sea. The lanterns came down in loose groups. Rei stood on the concrete embankment, past the steps where the families stood, where the river stopped being pretty and became a drain for the city. He smelled diesel and mud and watched the little lights drift past him.

This was the worst place to use his sight, and he had come here to use it. The membrane between the living and the dead was at its thinnest all week. It was thinnest of all over running water, at the festival of the dead. The moment he let the first register open a hand's width, the whole surface of the Sumida seemed to tilt. It stopped being a river with lanterns on it. It became a procession. A long, patient line of the departing moved with the current, and every paper flame had someone walking beside it.

He walked downstream, listening for the one wrong note among the dead. A man drowned three nights ago would be a wrong note. The properly dead were leaving this week. Kase was not leaving. Something was holding him.

Rei felt him before he saw anything, the way fingers find a snag in cloth. It was down past the third pier. There the current went slack behind a concrete footing, and any lantern that drifted in turned slow circles and did not come out again. His sight read the place as cold. His skin read it as nothing at all. Something in that slack water was keeping a man, the way the third basin had kept a half-made boy. It was not eating him yet. It was holding him, the way a person holds an object while they decide what to do with it.

And the held place was not silent. Tanizaki could not have prepared him for this part, and both registers leaned toward it with an old hunger Rei had always been told to refuse. It was leaking. A drowned man read this soon after death still carries his last quarter of an hour, the way a struck bell still holds its note. Rei could feel Kase's final minutes pressing out against the river's grip. The cold. The weight of his coat. A decision. A hand that was or was not on the back of his neck. All of it waited down there to be looked at. But looking was exactly what thinned the wall, and the wall over this water was already thin enough to put his fingers through.
The lanterns turned their slow circles behind the pier. One of them, Rei noticed, had no name written on its side at all.

Kase was where Rei knew he would be. He hung in the slack water behind the footing, one sleeve caught on a rusted steel rod. He was face down and turning slowly in the eddy, and his coat was as heavy as a drowned animal. Rei waded in up to his knees and took his wrist.

The river did not fight him. That was the first wrong thing, and the worst. A body held for three nights in slack water should belong to the river. Instead the current loosened its grip the moment Rei decided to take him, as if it had wanted Rei to have the body all along. Rei turned him over. Lantern light from upstream slid across his face. Drowning had been gentle with it. It was slack and almost untroubled, the face of a careful man who had stopped being careful at the very end. Then the last quarter of an hour, freed by Rei's touch, came off him into Rei's open register like cold coming off a stone.

Rei read it because he could not stop himself, and it was not the story Tanizaki had told him. Kase had not slipped. Kase had walked here barefoot in the dark, with the thing that frightened him buttoned inside his coat. The thing was a list. It was a small ledger wrapped in waxed paper. It recorded who in Kita had accepted a certain kind of favour in the last two years, and what each favour had quietly cost the membrane. Three nights too late, Kase had understood what carrying it made him. He was a loose thread in something very large and very patient. There was only one place in the city thin enough to lose the list, where no register could ever read it again. That was the bottom of the Sumida in Obon. He did not drown himself out of fear. He drowned himself to hide the ledger where even the dead could not be made to give it up. He walked in slowly, and this week the river was glad to keep them both.

And the keeper of the place was here. Rei had felt it the whole time, the way a person can feel someone watching from behind glass. It was not a demon and it was not a ghost. It was the slack water itself, grown aware. This stretch of Obon river had kept a hidden man and a hidden list for three nights, and in that time it had learned the taste of keeping secrets, the way still water learns things. It did not want Kase. It wanted the warm thing now kneeling in it with two registers open. It wanted the young man with a brother across the city, the brother it could feel him aching for. Without words, it offered to keep things for Rei too. It would take whatever he most needed hidden and hold it on the bottom. There no Healer and no Directorate and no patient thing in his brother's shape could ever read it out of him.
The ledger lay cold against the dead man's chest. The nameless lantern turned its slow circle by Rei's knee. The current waited to see what he would do with all three.

Rei gave the river nothing. He unbuttoned the coat with numb fingers. He took out the waxed packet and pushed it inside his own shirt, against his skin, where it was his to carry. Whatever he needed hidden, he would carry that too. He said so out loud, to the water. He felt foolish, and he said it again.

He got Kase out. That much he did not let himself bargain over. He laid him on the concrete above the tide line, under a courier's tarp that Tanizaki's network kept hidden nearby for nights like this. Then he knelt there dripping while the lanterns kept coming past the pier, name after name, floating out toward a sea that could not read them. The ledger sat heavy and cold against his chest. The slack water behind the footing had gone ordinary again. It was just river. The awareness in it had sunk back into the current the moment it failed to get what it offered to hold. Rei understood that he would never know whether he had outwitted it, or whether he had simply not been worth keeping.

Then there was the body, which was also the truth. A barefoot drowning in Obon was the most ordinary death in Tokyo. By morning a patrol would find him. The city's records would make him one more sad number for the season, and nobody would ever ask about a waxed ledger or the favours that cost the wall. Rei looked at the tarp and thought of the paired shoes by Kase's door. A man who left his shoes like that had already chosen how he wanted to go. He had wanted a lantern and a name. He had wanted to be off every book. Tanizaki had asked for the same thing, over a cup he did not drink.

The rain finally started, fine and warm. It dimpled the black water and made the nearer candles flicker. Rei climbed the steps to the last lantern seller, who was packing up her stall, and bought the one plain lantern she had left. He borrowed her brush and wrote KASE on its side. He wrote it badly, because his hand would not stay steady. He lit it and set it on the water at the footing, beside the nameless one. He gave the river back the man and kept the secret. The two lanterns turned once together in the slack water. Then the current took them both out into the procession. Kase left on his own terms.

Both registers were still half open and slow to close, the way they always were after running water. Through them Rei felt what he had really been doing down here. It was not a favour for an old man. He had come to the Sumida to practise the unbearable thing. To read a held person whom a patient power did not want to let go. To take a hidden truth, or refuse it. To kneel in a thin place and not be kept there. Somewhere across the city his brother was held exactly like this, in slack water of a different kind, by a Healer who was glad to keep him. Rei did not yet have the nerve or the method to go in after him. Kase had been a rehearsal. The knowledge sat in him as cold as the river. He could perhaps find Gin the way he had found this man. Finding was the easy half. The water did not always give up what a person meant to take.

He walked back to the tea shop in the last of the rain. The streets were empty except for a delivery scooter and a cat under a parked car, watching the water run in the gutter. A konbini on the corner glowed white, and the young clerk inside was stacking rice balls on a shelf for the morning. Rei's shoes squelched with every step. The sky over the river turned from black to grey.

blocks.cap: Tanizaki and Rei at dawn in the room above the tea shop

blocks.p: At dawn Tanizaki had set out two cups and filled three. It was the old custom, the third cup for the one who had gone. He did not explain it and Rei did not ask. Rei came in soaked to the knees with the night still on him and told him what he had found, all of it. Then he took the waxed packet out of his shirt and laid it on the table between the cups.

Tanizaki listened the way he listened to everything, without moving. He only turned his cup, the slow quarter-turn that meant he was rearranging forty years of knowledge about his district to fit a new and terrible fact. He did not open the packet. He laid his palm flat on it for a while, like a man feeling for a pulse.

When he finally spoke, he said something Rei did not expect. Kase had carried things for Gin too, years ago, the same kind of quiet errands in waxed paper. It was Gin who had taught the fixer the trick of hiding a thing in running water, where no register could reach it. "If Kase chose the Sumida," Tanizaki said, "he chose it because your brother once told him it was the one safe place." Even a fixer's chosen drowning had Gin's careful handwriting in the margin.

He poured the third cup out on the floor, the smallest offering. Then he told Rei what the old give the young when they have nothing else. The river takes everyone on its own terms in the end. The only mercy is to let a person choose those terms. Kase had done that, which was more than most of the dead this week had managed.
Rei asked the question he had carried up the stairs. "Is there anyone who could go in after Gin? Someone stronger than me. Stronger than the CVD."
Tanizaki was quiet long enough for the barley smell to come back into the room. "You mean a Master," he said.

Rei had heard the word all his life, used loosely, as praise for a good teacher. Tanizaki did not use it loosely. A Master, he said, was a Vanguard-rank independent. Vanguard was the top of the ranks a practitioner could reach. A Master was someone who had climbed past anything an institution could train, and then stepped out of its reach. The CVD called them unreliable, and from the CVD's side of the desk they were. They chose their own cases. They needed long rest between cases to stay stable at that height. They looked at patterns across years instead of weeks. And every one of them had paid something personal to get there. "The capability and the cost are the same thing," Tanizaki said. "Your brother wrote that down. He had watched three of them up close."
"Then I go to one of them."

"You consult one of them," Tanizaki said. "You do not deploy them. That is the first rule, and people break it every year and come home with nothing. The exchange is real. Whatever you take from a Master, you give back something of the same weight, and they will know if you cheat. Their cost is visible if you look, so look, and do not pretend afterwards that you did not see it. And respect what they will not tell you. There is always something. It is always for a reason you would not like." He touched the packet again. "Gin said the three he knew were not manageable. Then he added that he was including himself in that."

He did not thank Rei in words. Instead he slid four things across the table. The key to a safe house. His method for setting wards, written out in his own hand. The field profile he had kept on Gin since Gin was a boy, or the first part of it, in a cardboard folder gone soft with handling. And a single sheet folded in three, in Gin's handwriting, with a title Rei could read through the paper.

"Outside the doctrine," Tanizaki said. "Your brother's list of the people who still do the old work. Priests, a shaman, an elder. Houses the CVD walks past every day. Do not read it today. You will know the day you need it."

These were things he gave only when he trusted someone completely. Rei understood then that the drowned client had also been a test. He had passed it the hard way, by being trusted with a death that had to stay off the books. The rain had stopped. The barley smell was back. Outside, the dead had mostly gone home, and the lanterns had all reached the sea.

What stayed with Rei, as he walked out into the washed grey morning, was not the ledger or the key or even Kase's almost peaceful face. It was the small, hard lesson the river had handed up with the body. Hiding is a kind of drowning. A held thing can be loved into staying held. His brother had taught a fixer the safe place in the water. Now Gin was hidden in slack water of his own, and he had known this trick from the inside long before the Healer ever wore his coat. Tonight Rei had rehearsed the exact shape of what he would have to do for Gin. He had learned what it cost. He had learned that the water does not always give up what a person means to take. And he had decided to go in after him anyway.
The cup Tanizaki had poured for him had gone cold. He drank it. This morning it would have felt like an insult to leave anything behind that the river could keep.

On the stairs down to the street he felt the folded sheet in his pocket, Gin's handwriting pressed against his hip through the cloth. He did not take it out. Tanizaki had said he would know the day. Going out into the grey, Rei had the uneasy feeling that the day was already coming, and walking faster than he was.
